name.text: Module 3 · Lesson 10 · Section 1: Review of Lessons 1–9

questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lessons 1–9

Lesson 9 introduced the imperative (direct commands), the infinitive (verbal noun / maṣdar), and the l- + infinitive construction for expressing purpose, ability, desire, and obligation. Before proceeding, confirm you can recall the following:

  • Imperative formation: Peal msg = CCoC; fsg = CCoC+ī; mpl = CCoC+w; fpl = CCoC+ān

  • Negative commands: lā + imperfect (never imperative)

  • Infinitive: Peal = meCCaC; Paael = mCaCCāCū; Aphel = maCCāCū

  • Semi-modals: šarī, yākel, bāʿē, ṣābē, paqed, šadar — all govern l- + infinitive

name.text: Module 3 · Lesson 10 · Section 2: The Passive/Reflexive Stems — Overview

questiontext.text:
Section 2: The Passive/Reflexive Stems — Overview

2.1 The Principle of Passive Formation in Syriac

In Syriac, the passive voice is not expressed by auxiliary verbs (as in English: ‘is killed’, ‘was written’) but by a separate, inflected stem built from the active stem by means of a characteristic prefix: ʾEt- or Et-. These are called the Et-stems. Each active stem has a corresponding Et-stem that functions as its passive or reflexive counterpart.

Students of Hebrew will recognise an analogy with the Niphal (נִפְעַל, passive of Qal) and Hitpael (הִתְפַּעֵל, reflexive of Piel). Arabists will recognise the parallel with Forms V, VI, VII, and VIII: the tāʾ-prefixed (تَفَعَّلَ) and n-prefixed (اِنْفَعَلَ) passives/reflexives. In Greek, the same passive voice forms (e.g., παιδεύομαι) serve the function. Latin uses separate passive endings (-or, -ris, -tur etc.).

2.2 The Three Et-Stems

Et-Stem Name Active Counterpart Prefix Meaning / Function
Ethpeel ܐܬܦܥܠ Peal ʾet- Passive or reflexive of Peal: ‘to be killed’, ‘to wash oneself’
Etpaael ܐܬܦܥܠ Paael ʾetpa- Passive or reflexive of Paael: ‘to be blessed’, ‘to be sanctified’
Ettaphal ܐܬܐܦܥܠ Aphel ʾetta- Passive of Aphel (causative): ‘to be saved’, ‘to be sent’

Cross-Linguistic Summary: Passive Formation

Syriac Ethpeel: ʾet- + Peal root → parallel to Hebrew Niphal / Hitpael

Syriac Etpaael: ʾetpa- + Paael → parallel to Arabic Form V تَفَعَّلَ

Syriac Ettaphal: ʾetta- + Aphel → parallel to Arabic Form VII اِنْفَعَلَ

Greek: active + passive endings (same paradigm structure, different endings)

Latin: active vs. passive endings (-o/-or, -s/-ris, -t/-tur etc.)
How are the Syriac passive/reflexive stems formed?

answer.text: With the prefix ʾet- on the Peal, Paael or Aphel

name.text: Module 3 · Lesson 10 · Section 3: The Ethpeel Stem

questiontext.text:
Section 3: The Ethpeel Stem

3.1 Formation of the Ethpeel

The Ethpeel is formed by prefixing ʾet- to the Peal root. The perfect stem is ʾetCCeC. The participial form, which is very common, is metCCeC. In texts, the prefix may appear as ʾet- or ʾit- depending on dialect and vowelling.

Example: Root q-ṭ-l (kill) → Ethpeel perfect: ʾetqṭel ܐܬܩܛܠ ‘he was killed’; Participle: metqṭel ܡܬܩܛܠ ‘being killed’

3.2 Phonological Rules — Assimilation and Metathesis

When the Peal root begins with certain consonants, the t of the ʾet- prefix undergoes phonological changes:

  • Before sibilants (z, s, š, ṣ): Metathesis — the t and the sibilant swap positions. E.g., š-m-ʿ → ʾet-šmaʿ becomes ʾeš-t-maʿ ܐܫܬܡܥ ‘it was heard’; similarly ʾet-zʿaq → ʾez-t-ʿaq

  • Before dental/emphatic consonants (d, ṭ): Assimilation — the t assimilates to the following consonant. E.g., d-k-y → ʾet-dky becomes ʾed-dky (with doubling), sometimes written without the doubled letter.

  • Before all other consonants: No change — e.g., q-ṭ-l → ʾetqṭel; k-t-b → ʾetkatteb

3.3 Full Paradigm: Ethpeel of q-ṭ-l (be killed)

The t is dropped and then restored.

name.text: Module 3 · Lesson 10 · Section 4: The Ettaphal and Etpaael Stems

questiontext.text:
Section 4: The Ettaphal and Etpaael Stems

4.1 The Ettaphal — Passive of the Aphel

The Ettaphal is the passive counterpart of the Aphel (causative) stem. Its formation inserts ʾetta- before the root. Since the Aphel adds the causative meaning (‘to cause to X’), the Ettaphal means ‘to be caused to X’ — i.e., the passive of a causative, as in ‘to be saved’ (from ‘to save’), ‘to be sent’ (from ‘to send’).

Example 1: Root ḥ-y-y / Aphel ʾaḥyī (save/give life) → Ettaphal: ʾettaḥyī ܐܬܬܚܝ ‘he was saved / given life’

Example 2: Root ʾ-l-p / Aphel ʾalep (teach) → Ettaphal: ʾettalap ܐܬܬܠܦ ‘he was taught’

Example 3: Root ʾ-q-m / Aphel ʾaqīm (raise up) → Ettaphal: ʾettaqam ܐܬܬܩܡ ‘he was raised up’

Full Paradigm — Etpaael Perfect of š-d-r (be sent): (Paael šaddar ‘send’ → ʾeštaddar; before š the t of ʾet- swaps places with it)

Person / N / G Estrangela Transliteration Translation

4.2 The Etpaael — Passive/Reflexive of the Paael

The Etpaael is the passive or reflexive of the Paael (intensive/causative) stem. Its prefix is ʾetpa-. Since the Paael often carries intensive meaning (‘to bless greatly’, ‘to teach’), the Etpaael means ‘to be blessed’, ‘to be taught’, ‘to be sanctified’. It can also be reflexive (‘to sanctify oneself’).

Example 1: Root b-r-k / Paael barrek (bless) → Etpaael: ʾetbarrak ܐܬܒܪܟ ‘he was blessed’

Example 2: Root y-l-p / Paael yallep (teach) → Etpaael: ʾetyallap ܐܬܝܠܦ ‘he was taught / he learned’

Example 3: Root q-d-š / Paael qaddeš (sanctify) → Etpaael: ʾetqaddaš ܐܬܩܕܫ ‘he was sanctified / he sanctified himself’

name.text: Module 3 · Lesson 10 · Section 5: The Passive Participle (Peal)

questiontext.text:
Section 5: The Passive Participle (Peal)

5.1 Form and Usage

Distinct from the Ethpeel, the Peal passive participle is a simple adjectival form expressing a completed passive state: ‘written’ (ktīb), ‘killed’ (qṭīl), ‘bound’ (ʾsīr). Its pattern is CāCoC or in vocalized manuscripts CCīC. It agrees in gender and number with its noun, like any adjective. It is often used in verbless clauses with a predicative function: gawrā qṭīlā ܓܒܪܐ ܩܛܝܠܐ = ‘the man is killed / the killed man’.

Students of Arabic will recognise the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl): مَقْتُول maqṭūl ‘killed’, مَكْتُوب maktūb ‘written’. The Hebrew equivalent is qāṭūl: קָטוּל. The pattern is strikingly consistent across Semitic languages.

Section 7: The Story — Part 10

Yukhannan Is Thrown into the Fire — and Saved

The narrative continues from Lesson 9. Yukhannan has been bound and dragged to the furnace. Now the passive voice dominates the story: things happen to Yukhannan — he is thrown, he is saved, the miracle is revealed to the city. The story showcases Ethpeel, Ettaphal, and passive participle forms throughout.

And Yukhannan was thrown into the furnace. But the fire did not approach him — just as it was done with Hananiah and his companions. For a man of fire was seen in the midst of the furnace, and Yukhannan was illumined by his light. When he came out, his face was seen like the sun. All the crowd was gathered to see. And the great sign was made known in all the city. Many feared and repented. And they said: ‘Blessed is the God of Yukhannan!’ And Yukhannan was saved from the hands of his enemies, and glory was given to God.

Biblical Allusion: The reference to Ḥananyā and his companions (Hananiah/Shadrach — cf. Dan 3) is intentional. This is a common hagiographic motif in Syriac martyr literature: the saint re-enacts biblical miracles.
In the story, what happened when Yukhannan was thrown into the furnace?

answer.text: The fire did not approach him; he was unharmed.
He was badly burned but survived.

feedback.text: The fire did not touch him.

answer.text: He escaped before being thrown in.

questiontext.text: Which biblical parallel does the story draw?

answer.text: Hananiah and his companions in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3)

questiontext.text: What was seen in the midst of the furnace?

feedback.text: A man of fire was seen.

questiontext.text: How did the people respond, and what did they say?

answer.text: Many feared and repented, saying 'Blessed is the God of Yukhannan!' (brīk hū ʾAlāhā d-Yukhannan)
They mocked him, saying 'Where is your God?'

questiontext.text:
Section 10: Grammatical Summary Box

Complete Table of All Six Syriac Verbal Stems

This is the master reference table for all six Syriac stems. Memorise the patterns, the characteristic prefixes, and the cross-linguistic equivalents.

Stem Perf. 3msg Participle Prefix Meaning / Function
Peal ܦܥܠ qṭal ܩܛܠ qāṭel ܩܛܠ (none) Basic active: ‘he killed’
Paael ܦܥܠ qaṭtel ܩܛܠ mqaṭtel ܡܩܛܠ doubling Intensive / denominative: ‘he slew repeatedly / he executed’
Aphel ܐܦܥܠ ʾaqṭel ܐܩܛܠ maqṭel ܡܩܛܠ ʾa- Causative: ‘he caused to kill’
Ethpeel ܐܬܦܥܠ ʾetqṭel ܐܬܩܛܠ metqṭel ܡܬܩܛܠ ʾet- Passive/reflexive of Peal: ‘he was killed’
Etpaael ܐܬܦܥܠ ʾetqatṭal ܐܬܩܛܠ metqatṭal ܡܬܩܛܠ ʾetpa- Passive/reflexive of Paael: ‘he was executed’
Ettaphal ܐܬܐܦܥܠ ʾettaqṭal ܐܬܬܩܛܠ mettaqṭal ܡܬܬܩܛܠ ʾetta- Passive of Aphel: ‘he was caused to be killed’

Passive Participle Pattern

Peal Passive Participle

Pattern: CCīC (or CāCoC in some vocalization traditions)

Agrees in gender and number with noun (like any adjective)

m.sg.: ktīb ܟܬܝܒ | f.sg.: ktībtā ܟܬܝܒܬܐ | m.pl.: ktībīn | f.pl.: ktībān

Used predicatively in verbless clauses: gawrā qṭīlā = ‘the man is killed’

Compare: Arabic mafʿūl (مَكْتُوب maktūb ‘written’); Hebrew qāṭūl (קָטוּל)

Ethpeel Phonological Rules

Assimilation & Metathesis in Ethpeel

Before sibilants (z, s, š, ṣ): METATHESIS — t moves after the sibilant

ʾet- + š-m-ʿ → ʾeštmaʿ (not *ʾetšmaʿ)

Before dentals (d, ṭ): ASSIMILATION — t assimilates to the following letter

ʾet- + d-k-y → ʾeddkī

Before all other consonants: no change — ʾet- + q-ṭ-l → ʾetqṭel
